en: Thus have I heard: the Kosambiya Sutta, Discourse to the Monks of Kosambi, the forty-eighth in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time, the monks at Kosambī were living in strife, quarreling, and engaged in disputes, piercing one another with verbal daggers.
They could neither convince one another nor be convinced by others; they could neither persuade one another nor be persuaded by others.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, at Kosambī, the bhikkhus have taken to quarreling, brawling, and falling into disputes;
they dwell stabbing one another with the weapons of the tongue. They neither convince one another, nor do they accept being convinced.”
“They approach [the teacher], yet they do not inspire one another, nor do they attain mutual inspiration.
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, address those bhikkhus in my name, saying:”
“The Teacher summons you, venerable sirs.
“Very well, Bhante,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One, and he approached those bhikkhus. Having approached them, he said to those bhikkhus:
“The Teacher summons you, venerable sirs.”
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to that bhikkhu, and they approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there to one side, the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhus:
“Is it true, monks, that you are living having fallen into quarrels, disputes, and arguments, stabbing one another with the weapons of the tongue,
and that you neither persuade one another nor accept persuasion, neither convince one another nor accept conviction?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“What do you think, bhikkhus?
At the time when you are engaged in quarreling, brawling, and disputes, living while piercing one another with verbal weapons—
do you, at that time, maintain loving bodily action toward your fellow practitioners of the holy life?”
“Is loving verbal action … and loving mental action established both openly and in private toward your fellow practitioners?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Thus it seems, monks, at whatever time you live having fallen into quarrels, strife, and disputes,

stabbing one another with the weapons of the tongue, at that time neither loving bodily action nor loving verbal action nor loving mental action is established by you toward your fellow practitioners, both openly and in private.”
It is manifest among your fellow celibates both openly and in private.
Then why, you foolish men, knowing what and seeing what, do you live engaged in quarrels,
engaged in strife, fallen into disputes, piercing one another with verbal darts, neither persuading one another, nor...?
"Do not seek to win over others, do not cause one another to feel remorse, and do not resort to persuasion.
For that, O foolish men, will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, there are these six qualities that are memorable, which create affection, create respect, lead to being gathered together, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
What six?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu maintains bodily conduct imbued with loving-kindness toward his companions in the holy life, both openly and in private.”
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk maintains loving verbal conduct toward his fellow practitioners both openly and in private.
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk maintains a mind of loving-kindness toward his fellow celibates, both openly and in private.
This quality, too, is consoling, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to absence of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, whatever gains are righteous and righteously obtained—even if only the mere contents of an alms-bowl—[he shares them with his fellow celibates].
With such gains, he is one who shares his enjoyments without making private reservations, sharing them in common with virtuous companions in the holy life.
This quality, too, is consoling, creates affection, inspires respect, and leads to being gathered together, to lack of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk possesses those virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unspotted...

He dwells together with his fellow celibates in such virtues—virtues that are untarnished, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration—both openly and in private, sharing a commonality of virtue with them.
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and respectful; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells with his fellow celibates— both openly and in private— in conformity with that noble view which leads out, leading its practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering.
This too is a principle that is consoling, endearing, and inspiring, leading to inclusion, to non-contention, to harmony, and to unity.
“Monks, these six principles of cordiality create affection, create respect, lead to cohesion, non-dispute, harmony, and unity.

Of these six principles of cordiality, monks, this is the foremost, the most cohesive, the most unifying: namely, that noble view which leads out, which leads the one who practices it toward the complete destruction of suffering.
Just as, monks, for a gabled house, the pinnacle is the foremost, the most cohesive, and the most unifying.”
In the same way, monks, among these six principles of cordiality, this is the foremost, this is the cohesive, this is the unifying factor:

namely, that noble view which leads out, which leads the one who practices it toward the complete destruction of suffering. And how, monks, is that noble view which leads out, which leads the one who practices it toward the complete destruction of suffering? [It is as follows:]... [The discourse continues with the detailed exposition of the noble view.]...

Thus, monks, this is the noble view which leads out, which leads the one who practices it toward the complete destruction of suffering. In this way, monks, among these six principles of cordiality, this is the foremost, this is the cohesive, this is the unifying factor. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall undertake and practice these six principles of cordiality. It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves.
In this case, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
"Is there some obsession within me that is not yet abandoned, by which, with a mind obsessed by that obsession, I might not understand and see things as they truly are?
Monks, if a monk is obsessed by sensual lust, he is one whose mind is indeed obsessed.
If, monks, a monk is obsessed by ill will, his mind is indeed obsessed.
If, monks, a monk is obsessed by sloth and torpor, his mind is indeed obsessed.
If, monks, a monk is obsessed by restlessness and remorse, his mind is indeed obsessed.
If, monks, a bhikkhu is obsessed by doubt, his mind is indeed obsessed.
If, monks, a bhikkhu is intent on thinking about this world, his mind is indeed obsessed.
If, monks, a bhikkhu is intent on thinking about the other world, his mind is indeed obsessed.
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu dwells having become engaged in quarrels, disputes, and contention, piercing one another with verbal weapons, his mind is indeed obsessed.
He understands thus:
‘There is no obsession within me that is not abandoned, by which obsession my mind being obsessed, I might not understand and see things as they really are.’”
‘My mind is well-directed for the sake of awakening to the truths.
This is the first knowledge attained by him—noble, supramundane, and not shared with worldlings.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘By cultivating, developing, and frequently practicing this view, do I personally obtain tranquility and personally obtain extinguishment?
He understands thus:
‘By cultivating, developing, and frequently practicing this view, I personally obtain tranquility and personally obtain extinguishment.’
This is the second knowledge attained by him that is noble, supramundane, and not shared with worldlings.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘Is there any other ascetic or brahmin outside of this [teaching] who possesses a view such as I possess?’”
Thus he understands:
“There is no other ascetic or brahmin outside of this [teaching] who possesses such a view as I possess.
This is the third knowledge attained by him—noble, supramundane, and not shared by worldlings.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:
"Whatever nature a person endowed with right view possesses, I too possess that same nature.
And what, monks, is the nature possessed by a person endowed with right view?
This is the natural law, monks, for a person endowed with right view:
"Even if he commits such an offense for which a means of rehabilitation is known, he nevertheless quickly confesses, reveals, and discloses it to the Teacher or to wise fellow-celibates;
having confessed, revealed, and disclosed it, he undertakes restraint for the future."
“Just as, monks, a young child, weak and lying on its back, having stepped on a coal with its hand or foot, quickly withdraws it;
even so, monks, it is the natural law for a person endowed with right view:

‘Even if one commits such an offense for which a means of rehabilitation is known, one nevertheless quickly confesses, reveals, and discloses it to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.’”
Having taught, revealed, and made plain [the Dhamma], he undertakes restraint for the future.
He understands thus:
"Whatever nature a person endowed with right view possesses, I too possess that same nature."
This is the fourth knowledge attained by him: noble, supramundane, and not shared with worldlings.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:
"Whatever nature a person endowed with right view possesses, I too possess that same nature."
And of what nature, monks, is the natural law of a person who is accomplished in view?
This, monks, is the natural law for a person accomplished in view:

"Even though he may be diligent in those various high and low duties to be performed for his fellow celibates, he nevertheless has an intense longing for the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom."
“Just as, monks, a cow with a young calf licks both the post and nudges the calf,
even so, monks, it is the natural law for a person endowed with right view:

‘Even though he may apply himself zealously to those various high and low duties that are to be performed for his fellow celibates, he nevertheless has an intense longing for the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.’”
Thus he understands:
"Whatever nature a person endowed with right view possesses, I too possess that same nature.
This is the fifth knowledge attained by him—noble, supramundane, and not shared by worldlings.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:
“Whatever kind of strength a person endowed with right view possesses, I too possess that same kind of strength.
And what, monks, is the kind of strength a person endowed with right view possesses?

This, monks, is the strength of a person endowed with right view: when the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, they listen to the Dhamma with earnestness, with attention, with their whole heart, and with an attentive ear.
They understand thus:
"I am endowed with that same kind of strength with which a person endowed with right view is endowed."
This is the sixth knowledge attained by him—noble, supramundane, and not shared with worldlings.
Furthermore, monks, the noble disciple reflects thus:
“I am endowed with such strength as a person who is possessed of right view is endowed with.”
And of what kind, monks, is the strength with which a person accomplished in view is endowed?

This, monks, is the strength of a person accomplished in view: when the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, they gain knowledge of the meaning, they gain knowledge of the Dhamma, and they gain joy connected with the Dhamma.
They understand thus:
‘Just as a person endowed with right view possesses such power, so too do I possess such power.
This is the seventh knowledge attained by him—noble, supramundane, and not shared by worldlings.
Thus, monks, for a noble disciple endowed with these seven factors, the natural law conducive to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is well-established.
“Thus, monks, a noble disciple endowed with these seven factors is one who possesses the fruit of stream-entry.
This is what the Blessed One said.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Kosambiya Sutta, the eighth, is finished.
